newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: South Asia aims high with joint tourism promotion.
newsitem.headline: South Asia aims high with joint tourism promotion.

text.p: South Asia, offering attractions ranging from the snow-clad Himalayas to sun-drenched tropical beaches, may soon be able to carve itself a bigger slice of the global tourism market.
The New Delhi-based South Asian Travel & Tourism Exchange (SATTE) is holding a marketing convention in Sri Lanka in April aiming to boost the region's image abroad.
"South Asia's tourism potential is limitless," said Navin Berry, an Indian travel publisher who founded SATTE, the region's top travel mart, four years ago.
"It offers a vivid set of attractions spread across a wide region which is culturally and geographically so rich and diverse," Berry told Reuters on Wednesday.
Berry was in Colombo to organise SATTE 97, to be held from April 26-30, the first time the event has been held outside India.

The biggest tourism marketing event to be held in Sri Lanka is expected to provide a major boost to the host country, which has been hit by a 14-year civil war, local promoter Udaya Nanayakkara told Reuters.
The government says the war, which has pitted its forces against Tamil rebels seeking a separate homeland, has killed more than 50,000 people and eaten into its once lucrative tourist industry.
Tourism, once the Indian Ocean island's top foreign exchange earner, recorded a drop of 28 percent in arrivals in the 11 months to November, down to 266,436 people, the Ceylon Tourist Board said.
"SATTE is a major tourism event. Just holding such an event here will show the world that Sri Lanka is safe for tourism," said the board's director of marketing, Vipula Wanigasekera.

Nanayakkara said SATTE was inspired by the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC), which groups seven countries -- India, Pakistan, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Bhutan and the Maldives.
"SAARC wants to promote liberal movement of tourism traffic across member countries' borders. It believes in the joint exploitation of the region's tourism potential," Nanayakkara said.
SATTE planned to promote, package and sell the region jointly, offering an array of previously unheard of package tours, Berry said.
"The industry is already talking about traversing the Himalayas in a novel way. You start from Pakistan, go through Nepal and conclude your journey in Bhutan," he said.
"A tourist will soon be able to cruise the Indian Ocean, making stops in India, Sri Lanka and the Maldives," he added.
